conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’ll be walking you through a short questionnaire called the **EPDS** (Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale). It’s simply a 10-question check-in about how you’ve been feeling in the past seven days—nothing fancy, just a way for us to see how motherhood is treating you emotionally and to be sure we’re not missing anything that might need extra support.  

Everything you share stays between you, me, and the clinical team; we want you to feel completely safe and un-rushed. After we finish the questions I’ll tally the results, let you know what they mean, and we can talk about any next steps that feel right for you. Ready to start?  

First, thinking about the past week: have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult lately?

I’ve still been able to laugh—maybe not quite as easily as before the baby, but when my partner makes a silly joke or when I see the dog doing something goofy, I do laugh. It just takes a tiny bit more effort, I guess.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Yeah, that sounds right—I can still laugh and see the funny side of things.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things
I do still look forward to things—like my morning coffee or taking the baby out in the stroller—though sometimes I’m so tired that the excitement is a little muted.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Not really. If the baby spits up right after I’ve changed him or I can’t get the swaddle tight enough on the first try, I might mutter “ugh, my bad,” but I don’t sit there thinking I’m a terrible mom or keep replaying it in my head. Stuff just happens with babies, and I move on.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

A little bit, yeah. Most of the time it’s just tiny stuff—like I’ll suddenly wonder if the baby’s breathing when he’s napping, even though I can see the monitor is fine. It’s not constant and it doesn’t take over my day, but it pops up for no real reason.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
No, I haven’t felt scared or panicky—nothing like that.
Things have been getting on top of me

Sometimes, yeah. Like yesterday—he wouldn’t settle after the three-a.m. feed, laundry was piled up, and I still hadn’t eaten. For a minute it felt as if everything were stacked on my shoulders, but I took a breath, put him in the sling, and the day moved along. It passes pretty quickly.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping
No, that hasn’t happened. I sleep pretty well—pretty much whenever the baby lets me. I’m tired, sure, but not because I’m lying there feeling unhappy.
I have felt sad or miserable
Not really. I get a little teary once in a while when I’m extra tired, but it’s short-lived—just a moment—and then I’m back to feeling okay.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
No, I haven’t felt that kind of unhappy. I might get a bit weepy when I’m really tired, but it’s not the “can’t-stop-crying” sort of thing—just a quick tear or two and then I’m fine.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. That hasn’t crossed my mind at all.

You've shared that life with your new baby is mostly going well: you still laugh at your partner's jokes, look forward to small pleasures like coffee or stroller walks, and move on quickly from everyday hiccups. You do notice the occasional, fleeting wave of worry about the baby's breathing and a brief sense of being overwhelmed when sleep and chores pile up, but these feelings pass within minutes and don't cloud your overall mood. You're tired, yet you sleep when the baby allows and you haven't felt persistently sad, panicky, or hopeless.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 5, Risk Level: Depression not likely (concerns include <sym>Patient reports recurring, unprovoked worries about the baby's safety that occur "for no real reason," matching "Yes, sometimes" despite being described as "tiny stuff."</sym>)
**Reasoning:** Score of 5 falls below the 8-point threshold; only Q4 and Q6 endorsed mildly. No core symptoms of persistent low mood, anhedonia, guilt, sleep disruption due to mood, or self-harm thoughts. Responses do not meet <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med> which requires ≥5 symptoms (including depressed mood or loss of interest) for 2 weeks, plus clinically significant distress or impairment. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Continue routine well-baby and postpartum check-ups
2. Re-screen with EPDS in 2-4 weeks or sooner if mood, worry, or functioning worsens
3. Practice rest-when-baby-sleeps and accept help with chores to reduce fatigue
4. Use brief relaxation techniques (deep breathing, 5-minute shower) when <sym>overwhelm</sym> surfaces
5. Share any new or worsening feelings with your <med>primary care provider</med> at once
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 5: Screening Note – Postpartum Visit  
Date: [today]

Source: Patient self-report on 10-item postpartum screen.

Symptoms endorsed  
• Transient, situational tearfulness when fatigued (Q8, Q9)  
• Occasional “things getting on top of me” that resolves quickly (Q6)  
• Mild, brief anxiety spikes re: infant safety without objective trigger (Q4)

Symptoms denied  
Persistent low mood, loss of pleasure, guilt/worthlessness, sleep disruption related to mood, panic, self-harm ideation.

Pattern  
Overall affective state stable; momentary fatigue-related distress without functional impairment. No evidence of sustained depressive or anxiety syndrome; no safety concerns identified.

Risk screening  
Current findings below threshold for postpartum depression or anxiety disorder; no red-flag items (self-harm, hopelessness, inability to function). Continue routine support/education; re-screen if symptoms worsen or persist.
